passages.happening:
‘King Solomon, however, loved many foreign women along with the daughter of Pharaoh’ (verse 1): women of Moab, Ammon, Edom and Sidon, and Hittite women. They came from the nations of which the LORD had told Israel, “You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods” (verse 2). ‘Yet Solomon clung to these women in love’ (verse 2). ‘He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines’ (verse 3).

“For when Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods, and he was not wholeheartedly devoted to the LORD his God, as his father David had been” (verse 4). He follows Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Milcom of the Ammonites (verse 5). On a hill east of Jerusalem he builds a high place for Chemosh of Moab and for Molech of the Ammonites, and he does the same for all his foreign wives, who burn incense and sacrifice to their gods (verses 7-8).

The LORD is angry with Solomon, ‘because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice’ (verse 9). God tells him that he will tear the kingdom from him and give it to his servant. But for David's sake he will not do it in Solomon's lifetime, and he will not take all of it: one tribe will remain for Solomon's son, ‘for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, which I have chosen’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The warning of chapter 9 begins to come true. The king who dedicated the temple builds high places for Chemosh and Molech within sight of it, and the golden age of chapters 3 to 10 ends in a single chapter.

Royal marriages in the ancient world were political. A foreign princess sealed a treaty, and she brought her household and her gods with her. Seven hundred wives of royal birth describe a vast web of alliances; three hundred concubines were wives of lower rank. Building a shrine for a wife's national god was ordinary courtesy among kings. For Israel it was exactly what the law forbade, since Deuteronomy had warned that such marriages would turn Israel's heart to other gods.

The concern in the text is worship, not birth. Ruth the Moabite, David's own ancestor, had joined herself to Israel's God.

The gods are named. Chemosh was the god of Moab, named on the Mesha Stele, where King Mesha credits him with his victories over Israel. Milcom was the national god of Ammon. Ashtoreth was a goddess of the Phoenician coast. Later books tie the worship of Molech to the burning of children, which the law calls detestable; this chapter says only that Solomon built him a high place.

The word heart runs through the chapter (verses 2, 3, 4 and 9). The verb for Solomon's clinging, davaq, is the one Deuteronomy uses for Israel clinging to the LORD. It shows what took God's place.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy had warned that a king ‘must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray’ (Deuteronomy 17:17). Josiah, about three centuries later, desecrated the high places Solomon built east of Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:13), and he desecrated the place where children were burned ‘so that no one could sacrifice his son or daughter in the fire to Molech’ (2 Kings 23:10).

Proverbs, linked with Solomon's name, gives the counsel he did not keep: “Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23).
passages.hard:
How could the wisest man in Israel end like this, and are seven hundred wives meant literally?

The text does not treat wisdom as a guarantee of faithfulness. It says that Solomon's heart turned when he grew old, slowly and through his loves. Many readers find this the chapter's sharpest lesson: knowing what is right and loving it with a whole heart are different things. Proverbs, linked with Solomon's name, warns again and again of the very danger that undid him.

As for the numbers, some scholars think they are inflated royal language, as the counts of other ancient royal households sometimes were. Others take them as a real count of marriages made for treaties over forty years. Either way the narrator's point stands. The king broke the law for kings on a scale no one could miss, and the result was the one that law foretold: his heart went astray.

The women themselves are not named in this chapter, and they are given no voice. They were sent as seals on treaties and gathered into a king's house. The text says that his wives turned his heart, but the verdict falls on Solomon himself: he clung to them, he built the high places, and he did not keep the LORD's command (verses 2, 9-11).
passages.asks: Solomon's heart turned slowly, through what he loved. Ask what you love that is pulling your heart, little by little, away from God. And ask what you have built room for in your life that you once would never have allowed.

passages.happening:
“Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite, from the royal line of Edom” (verse 14). Years before, when Joab led David's army in Edom, Hadad, then a young boy, had escaped to Egypt with some of his father's servants (verses 15-17). Pharaoh gave him a house, land and food, and his wife's sister in marriage, and Hadad's son grew up in Pharaoh's palace (verses 18-20). When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead, he asked Pharaoh to let him go home (verses 21-22).

‘And God raised up against Solomon another adversary, Rezon the son of Eliada’ (verse 23). Rezon had fled from his master, the king of Zobah, gathered a band of raiders and taken Damascus (verse 24). ‘Rezon was Israel’s enemy throughout the days of Solomon’ (verse 25), and he ruled over Aram.
passages.hearers:
The word for adversary is satan, used here as an ordinary noun for an opponent. Only in a few later texts, such as Job 1 and 2 and Zechariah 3, does it describe a heavenly accuser, and later still it becomes a name. Reading the devil into this chapter would be a mistake. The irony is plain all the same. Solomon had told Hiram that there was no adversary (5:4), and now God raises up adversaries, with that very word.

Hadad was an Edomite prince who escaped the killing in Edom that 2 Samuel records. The Egyptian queen Tahpenes is not named in surviving Egyptian sources, and her pharaoh is not identified. Rezon took Damascus, which from this point becomes the center of the Aramean kingdom that will trouble Israel for two centuries.

The edges of Solomon's power are fraying, south and north, while he is still alive.
passages.later: 2 Samuel records David's conquest of Edom: ‘He placed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites were subject to David’ (2 Samuel 8:14). Job uses the same word for an accuser in heaven: ‘and Satan also came with them’ (Job 1:6).
passages.asks: Solomon had said there was no adversary, and two arose while he was still on the throne. Ask where you have counted on a peace that depended on your own faithfulness. And ask whether old wrongs, like the war in Edom, still have consequences you have not faced.

passages.t: Jeroboam, and a cloak torn in twelve
passages.happening:
Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite whose mother was a widow, is one of Solomon's servants, and he rebels against the king (verse 26). Solomon had seen how hard the young man worked and put him in charge of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph (verses 27-28).

One day, as Jeroboam leaves Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah of Shiloh meets him alone in the open country, wearing a new cloak. “And Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing, tore it into twelve pieces” (verse 30), and said, “Take ten pieces for yourself” (verse 31). The LORD will tear the kingdom from Solomon's hand and give Jeroboam ten tribes, because the people have forsaken him to worship Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom (verses 31-33). One tribe will remain for David's sake and for Jerusalem's, ‘so that My servant David will always have a lamp before Me in Jerusalem’ (verse 36). If Jeroboam listens and walks in God's ways as David did, God will be with him and build him ‘a lasting dynasty just as I built for David’ (verse 38). “Because of this, I will humble David’s descendants” (verse 39), God says, and it will not be forever.

Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Shishak king of Egypt and stays there until Solomon dies (verse 40). The rest of Solomon's acts are written ‘in the Book of the Acts of Solomon’ (verse 41). He reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years. He dies, and his son Rehoboam reigns in his place (verses 42-43).
passages.hearers:
Jeroboam is a capable man from Ephraim, put in charge of the labor gangs of the house of Joseph, the central tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. He knows the north's grievances from the inside.

Tearing a garment was a way of acting out a prophecy, a sign-act that made the word visible and, in the ancient understanding, set it in motion. It recalls the robe torn when the kingdom was torn from Saul. The word tear runs through the chapter: God will tear the kingdom, and Ahijah tears his new cloak.

Twelve pieces, ten for Jeroboam, and one tribe for David's son. The text leaves one piece unexplained, and in chapter 12 Benjamin goes with Judah (12:21). What matters is the promise: a lamp, a picture of a family line kept alive, still burning in Jerusalem.

Jeroboam is offered a lasting dynasty on the same terms as David's: listen, walk in God's ways, keep his statutes. Shishak, to whom he flees, is Sheshonq I, founder of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty, who reigned about 945 to 924 BC. He is the first pharaoh the Bible names, and his name is one of the fixed points for dating this period.

The closing lines set the pattern the book will use for every king who follows: the sources, the length of the reign, death, burial and successor. The Book of the Acts of Solomon was a royal source, now lost.
passages.later: Samuel had said to Saul, ‘The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor’ (1 Samuel 15:28). And a psalm keeps the promise of the lamp: ‘I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one’ (Psalm 132:17).
passages.hard:
Why does God tear the kingdom from Solomon's son, and not from Solomon?

The text says it plainly. For David's sake the judgment will not come in Solomon's lifetime (verse 12), and the kingdom will not be torn away entirely; one tribe will remain (verse 13). The promise to David holds even when David's son breaks faith. God judges Solomon's unfaithfulness, and he keeps his word to David. Ahijah's last line looks further still: David's line will be humbled, but not forever.

Some readers find it hard that the loss falls in the son's days. The text does not say that Rehoboam loses the kingdom only for his father's sin; chapter 12 shows him making his own foolish choice. The judgment works through human decisions, and God is not the author of the sins involved.
passages.asks: Jeroboam was offered what David had, on David's terms. Ask what God has offered you, and on what terms. And ask what it means to you that God keeps a lamp burning for the sake of someone else's faithfulness.
